title: Trigger submission never executes — keeper logs attempt then silently skips
description: runOnePollCycle is the ONLY thing main()'s production loop calls. After logTriggerAttempt, the function ends with the comment '// Note: trigger submission requires a signer ... we skip submission.' main() never invokes signAndSubmitTrigger, never constructs a signer, never calls buildTriggerTransaction. The keeper therefore emits trigger_attempt log lines but never fires a transaction, never logs trigger_fired, never logs trigger_failed. The 'fire path' is dead code at runtime.
impact: AC3.10 unsatisfied at runtime — the keeper detects but does not fire. AC3.12 keeper-side prerequisite (the 'detects-and-fires' leg) is broken: the operator pushes the price, the keeper logs trigger_attempt, then nothing happens on-chain. The structured-log error path (trigger_failed / abort code parsing) is unreachable because submission never happens. Operators have no signal that the keeper is mis-wired beyond noticing the missing trigger_fired lines.
recommendation: Wire signAndSubmitTrigger into the production path: construct the Ed25519 signer once at boot, plumb it into a non-test variant of the poll cycle, and on shouldFire build+sign+submit the trigger. Wrap in try/catch that calls logTriggerFailed with the abort code parsed from the SDK error string. Then mark the vault triggered ONLY after a successful response. Either remove the test-seam comment (and run real submission inside runOnePollCycle behind an injected signer) or expose a separate runOnePollCycleWithSigner that production uses.
evidence:
// Note: trigger submission requires a signer, which is only available
      // in the full boot path. In runOnePollCycle (test seam), we skip submission.

title: Silent catch on price calculation hides Pyth staleness, paused feeds, and overflow
description: calculateBaseQuotePrice throws 'zero magnitude' (paused or unpublished Pyth feed) and 'price overflow u64' (degenerate exponents). The catch block here is { continue; } with no log, no counter, no diagnostic. A vault whose pool prices are stale or paused is silently skipped every poll cycle forever. The dimension-prompt's Pyth-trust caveat (the keeper supplies current_price trustfully) is exactly the case this swallowed exception undermines: operators have no way to know the keeper is failing to evaluate.
impact: Silent data loss: triggers that SHOULD fire don't, because the price wasn't computable. Operators see periodic poll_cycle lines with prices but no trigger_attempt / trigger_fired and assume the price hasn't crossed the threshold. The contract requires a pyth_read_failed line on Pyth read failure; the analogous price-formula failure is invisible.
recommendation: Replace the empty catch with a structured log: emit a new 'price_calc_failed' event (or reuse pyth_read_failed with the vault_id field) carrying { vault_id, base_object_id, quote_object_id, error }. Continue iteration but make the failure visible.

title: All vaults priced with hardcoded DEEP-as-base SUI-as-quote regardless of pool
description: The price-pair resolution comment says 'For now, use DEEP oracle for base and SUI oracle for quote on the DEEP/SUI pool' and then DOES exactly that for every vault in the registry. There is no resolution from manifest.pools[] to the correct (basePriceInfoObjectId, quotePriceInfoObjectId) pair. A vault on the SUI/USDC pool would be priced with the DEEP/SUI formula, producing a wrong current_price and either a spurious fire or a silent miss. The contract explicitly requires manifest-driven pool→price-pair resolution per Behavior step 2.
impact: Wrong-price triggers on any non-DEEP/SUI pool. Owner who set TP=1.0 USDC/SUI gets fired at a price computed from DEEP/USD oracles. Funds get swapped on bogus signals. This is a correctness break that surfaces as an error-handling failure: the keeper does not detect or refuse the mismatch — it silently does the wrong thing.
recommendation: Resolve each vault's pool_id against manifest.pools[] to learn (basePriceInfoObjectId, quotePriceInfoObjectId, baseDecimals, quoteDecimals) before computing current_price. If the vault's pool_id is not in the manifest, log a structured 'pool_unknown' warning and skip the vault. Do not silently fall back to DEEP/SUI.

title: Vault discovery RPC errors written to stderr, not surfaced as structured log events
description: When discoverVaultsTick throws (RPC down, malformed response, query error), the catch block does process.stderr.write of an unstructured string. The AC3.11 logging contract requires line-delimited JSON on stdout for every observable behavior. There is no 'vault_discovery_failed' event in the schema and no structured representation here, so a downstream parser (Cycle 5 UI / E-007 harness) cannot detect an outage of the discovery loop — they only see poll_cycle lines proceed normally with stale registry contents.
impact: Operator visibility into a discovery-loop outage is degraded. A keeper whose RPC is briefly broken keeps logging poll_cycle with known_vault_count stuck at the last value; the actual cause (RPC errors) is in stderr, which structured log consumers don't read. Cycle 1's R3-007 'isolate per-vault' lesson called out exactly this failure pattern; this is the same regression at the discovery layer.
recommendation: Add a structured 'vault_discovery_failed' event to logger.ts with { error } and emit it here. Keep the per-cycle continue behavior. Optionally count consecutive failures and escalate after N to keeper_shutdown.

title: Malformed VaultCreated event silently dropped — empty catch with no log
description: parseVaultCreatedEvent throws a descriptive error when any of the seven required fields is missing (per its own contract). The caller swallows that exception with `} catch { /* Skip malformed events */ }` — no log line, no counter, no event id captured. A schema drift between the Move contract and the keeper (e.g., a field renamed in a future Cycle 3 amendment, or a chain-side malformation) becomes invisible.
impact: A vault that should have been registered is silently absent from the registry. The owner's TP/SL never fires. Operator sees no trigger_attempt and no diagnostic. The descriptive error message that parseVaultCreatedEvent worked hard to construct is discarded.
recommendation: Replace the empty catch with: emit a structured 'vault_event_parse_failed' warn line with { tx_digest, event_seq, error }. The downstream parser can correlate the missing vault with a parse failure. Continue iterating other events as today.

title: SIGINT/SIGTERM handler does not drain in-flight transactions despite contract promise
description: Contract Lifecycle section says 'install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that stop the two loops, drain in-flight transactions, log a keeper_shutdown line, and exit zero.' Implementation immediately calls process.exit(0) inside the signal handler. There is no await on any in-flight promise; the running flag is set to false but never checked between exit and the next loop iteration; an in-progress signAndSubmitTrigger (once R3-001 is fixed) would be killed mid-flight. Additionally, both handlers can fire reentrantly (no idempotency guard).
impact: An in-flight execute_trigger that was signed and submitted but whose result we have not yet read could leave the on-chain state ahead of the keeper's belief: vault.triggered is true on-chain, false in the (now-dead) keeper memory. On restart, seedTriggeredFromChain (which is also unwired — see related findings) would be needed to recover. A second SIGINT during shutdown re-enters the handler and double-emits keeper_shutdown.
recommendation: Make the handler async-friendly: set running=false, await an in-flight tracker (Promise.allSettled over outstanding submits with a timeout), then logKeeperShutdown and exit. Guard against reentry with a `let shuttingDown = false` flag.

title: Pyth getObject RPC error not checked — silently falls through to fabricated initial_shared_version=1n
description: After fetch(rpcUrl, ...) for sui_getObject, the response is parsed without checking resp.ok and without checking getObjJson.error. If the RPC returns an error envelope (e.g. object not found, RPC schema drift, oracle service stopped), getObjJson.result is undefined, rawVersion is undefined, and initialSharedVersion silently defaults to `1n`. This fabricated version is then passed to devInspect, where the failure surfaces as a confusing 'shared object initial version mismatch' error rather than the actual 'PriceInfoObject not found' diagnosis.
impact: Misleading error messages when the oracle-service is not running (which the contract's escalation triggers explicitly call out). Operator sees devInspect failures and chases the wrong root cause. The G-Pyth escalation pathway is undermined because the actual failure is masked.
recommendation: Check resp.ok and getObjJson.error explicitly. On error or missing data.owner.Shared.initial_shared_version, throw a clear error that names the priceInfoObjectId and the underlying RPC failure. Do not fabricate a default version.
evidence:
const rawVersion = getObjJson.result?.data?.owner?.Shared?.initial_shared_version;
  const initialSharedVersion = rawVersion !== undefined ? BigInt(rawVersion) : 1n;

title: No fetch timeout anywhere in keeper — single hung RPC stalls entire poll loop
description: Every fetch() call in pythReader.ts, triggerSubmitter.ts, and index.ts (discoverVaultsTick) is bare — no AbortController, no timeout, no signal. A hung TCP socket against the local RPC (or, in less benign environments, against a misbehaving full node) blocks the await indefinitely. Because the main poll loop is a sequential while loop with `await runOnePollCycle(...)`, a single hung Pyth read freezes the entire keeper: no further poll_cycle lines, no trigger evaluation for any vault, no shutdown response to SIGTERM (since the await is not interruptible).
impact: Liveness failure mode that looks like a successful keeper from a glance at the process table. Triggers stop firing across all vaults. The structured log goes silent (no error, no progress). Recovery requires SIGKILL since SIGTERM is not picked up while await is blocked.
recommendation: Wrap each fetch with a per-call AbortController bounded by a sub-second-of-poll-interval timeout (e.g., 2000ms). On timeout, throw and let the caller's catch path emit pyth_read_failed / vault_discovery_failed structured lines. Optionally add a watchdog timer in the main loop that kills the process if a single tick exceeds 3x pollIntervalMs.

title: No staleness check on Pyth publishTimeSeconds despite trust-design carry-forward
description: parsePriceFromBcs returns publishTimeSeconds, and notes/pyth-shape.md per the contract documents it as 'parsed but not enforced'. The Cycle 3 carry-forward concern (the Move contract trusts the keeper-supplied current_price wholesale) means the keeper is the ONLY defense against stale or paused oracles. Yet nothing in runOnePollCycle compares publishTimeSeconds to wall clock or to the previous poll's value. A paused feed returning the same price for 10 minutes would still be passed through to execute_trigger, which would fire on stale data.
impact: If oracle-service silently stops publishing, the keeper continues firing triggers on the last-known price until somebody notices. Owner gets executed at a price the market has since moved away from. This is the exploit class the dimension prompt explicitly flagged ('what if Pyth feed is stale or paused? Keeper should detect').
recommendation: After parsePriceFromBcs, compare publishTimeSeconds to Date.now()/1000. If older than a configurable max-age (e.g., 60 seconds default), emit a structured 'pyth_stale' warn line and treat the read as a failure (skip evaluation for vaults that depend on this oracle). Document the threshold in notes/pyth-shape.md (the file already says staleness is out of scope but the dimension prompt says detection is required).
evidence:
// A note on staleness: `publish_time` is parsed and exposed
//   but the keeper does NOT enforce a max-age check this cycle

title: signAndSubmitTrigger missing HTTP-status check and gas-price fallback hides errors
description: Two issues in the gas-price fetch path: (1) gasPriceResp.ok is never checked. A 5xx from the RPC returns an HTML body that fails JSON.parse silently (or returns gasPriceJson.result undefined). (2) On undefined result, the keeper silently substitutes 1000n MIST as the gas price. If the network's reference gas price is higher, transactions get rejected with confusing 'gas price too low' errors that look like a Move abort rather than an RPC outage.
impact: Trigger submissions fail with the wrong error message when the RPC is degraded; the abort_code_or_message logged in trigger_failed misleads the operator. The fabricated 1000n is also a magic number not tied to any documented localnet value.
recommendation: Check resp.ok and gasPriceJson.error. On any failure throw a clear 'reference gas price unavailable' error so the upstream catch logs trigger_failed with an actionable abort_code_or_message. Do not fabricate a default gas price.
evidence:
const gasPriceJson = (await gasPriceResp.json()) as { result?: string };
  const gasPrice = gasPriceJson.result ? BigInt(gasPriceJson.result) : 1000n;

title: Logger secret redaction shallow — does not recurse into nested objects or arrays
description: buildLine iterates Object.entries(extra) at the top level only and skips keys in SECRET_KEYS. If a caller passes `{ keeper: { secretKey: '...' } }` or `{ keypairs: [{ privateKey: '...' }] }`, the redaction does not apply — the nested secret is serialized to stdout. Spec says 'never logged in full' for the ephemeral keypair, and the Logger T-007 test only validates top-level redaction, leaving the nested case untested.
impact: Defense-in-depth gap. If a future patch passes a richer 'response' or 'context' object that happens to contain a privateKey field (e.g., serializing a full keypair object for debug), the secret leaks to stdout. The keeper key is ephemeral so the blast radius is small on localnet, but the rule exists for a reason and the implementation does not honor it.
recommendation: Make redaction recursive: a serializer that walks objects and arrays, omitting any key in SECRET_KEYS at any depth. Or simpler — implement a JSON.stringify replacer that drops secret keys at every depth.

title: vaultRegistry uses console.warn instead of structured logger — bypasses AC3.11 contract
description: seedTriggeredFromChain emits warnings via console.warn(JSON.stringify(...)) directly to stderr. This bypasses the structured logger module, hard-codes a one-off event name 'seed_triggered_warning' that is not in AC3.11's enumerated list, and uses stderr instead of the contract-mandated stdout-only channel. Operators parsing stdout for events will miss these.
impact: A vault whose on-chain content is malformed or missing produces a warning the structured-log consumer never sees. Defaults to triggered=false silently, which means restart-after-fire would re-attempt a doomed trigger (the exact scenario contract decision #3 was meant to prevent).
recommendation: Add a 'seed_triggered_warning' (or rename to 'vault_seed_failed') event to logger.ts and call it from here. Inject the logger as a dependency to keep the registry pure-ish, or import it directly.
evidence:

        JSON.stringify({
          ts: new Date().toISOString(),
          level: 'warn',
          event: 'seed_triggered_warning',

title: seedTriggeredFromChain never called on startup — restart-after-fire will re-attempt doomed trigger
description: Contract decision #3 explicitly says 'On startup, before entering the trigger loop, the keeper SHOULD re-read each known vault's on-chain state via client.getObject(vaultId) (with showContent: true) and seed triggered from there; without this seeding, a keeper restart immediately after a fire would attempt a doomed-to-abort execute_trigger retry.' The implementation in main() never calls registry.seedTriggeredFromChain. After a restart, the registry rebuilds from VaultCreated events with triggered=false on every entry; the next price tick would attempt to re-fire triggers on already-fired vaults. Each attempt would abort on-chain with EVaultTriggered, costing gas and DEEP per cycle until the operator notices.
impact: On restart of a keeper that fired triggers in a prior run, every already-triggered vault generates a doomed execute_trigger on the next poll. With one DEEP per attempt and a default 5-second poll interval, this burns DEEP indefinitely (no blacklisting per contract spec — the abort doesn't suppress retries). Operator sees a flood of trigger_failed lines with EVaultTriggered abort codes (assuming R3-001 is fixed first; today the bug is masked by the no-submission bug).
recommendation: After the discovery loop catches up to live and before the first price tick, iterate the registry and await registry.seedTriggeredFromChain for each known vault. Wrap in Promise.allSettled to tolerate partial RPC failures. Log a 'seed_complete' info line when done.

title: Boot-time errors crash with unstructured console.error — no keeper_failed_to_start event
description: If loadConfig throws on bad env, or fs.readFileSync throws on missing manifest, or Ed25519Keypair construction throws, the catch at the bottom of the file does console.error('Fatal error:', err) and process.exit(1). The structured-log consumer (Cycle 5 UI / E-007 harness) cannot distinguish 'keeper crashed at boot' from 'keeper never started' because no log line is emitted to stdout. AC3.11 enumerates keeper_started and keeper_shutdown but no boot-failure event.
impact: Diagnosability gap. Cycle 5's UI cannot present a 'keeper failed to boot — check env' message because it has no structured signal. Operators must SSH and look at stderr to see the actual config error.
recommendation: Add a 'keeper_failed_to_start' error event to logger.ts and emit it before exiting. Include { error } so the consumer can render the cause. Keep exit code 1.

title: parsePriceFromBcs accepts 34-byte exact match but does not warn on length-mismatch overshoot
description: The check is `if (bytes.length < PRICE_BCS_LENGTH) throw`. If devInspect returns 35+ bytes (e.g., upstream Pyth bumps the Price struct, adding a new field — exactly the G-Pyth escalation trigger), the decoder reads the first 34 bytes silently and ignores the rest. The upstream layout drift is not detected; the trailing bytes get discarded. The G-Pyth gate's whole purpose is to surface this kind of drift.
impact: If the bundled Pyth package is upgraded mid-cycle and the Price struct grows a field, the keeper silently mis-decodes and either reads wrong values or reads correct values but misses new defense-relevant fields (e.g., a status flag indicating the feed is paused).
recommendation: Tighten the check to `bytes.length !== PRICE_BCS_LENGTH` and throw with a clear 'BCS layout drift detected: expected 34 bytes, got N — see notes/pyth-shape.md and re-capture' message. The G-Pyth escalation pathway then fires as designed.

title: evaluateTrigger has no try/catch in caller — unexpected vault shape kills the entire vault loop
description: evaluateTrigger is pure and accepts bigints, but if a malformed vault somehow has a non-bigint tp_price (e.g., post-restart deserialization corruption, upstream parser bug), the comparison `currentPrice >= vault.tp_price` throws TypeError. The for-loop has no inner try/catch, so a single bad vault aborts iteration and the rest of the vaults are skipped this tick. This is the Cycle 1 R3-007 'isolate per-vault' lesson the dimension prompt called out.
impact: One corrupt registry entry stops trigger evaluation for every other vault each tick. The outer try in main() catches and continues, so the keeper survives; but the affected tick produces no trigger_attempt for the healthy vaults, delaying their fires by one poll interval (every poll interval, until the bad vault is removed).
recommendation: Wrap the loop body in try/catch; on error log a structured 'vault_eval_failed' warn with { vault_id, error } and continue to the next vault.
evidence:
for (const vault of registry.iterate()) {
    if (!vault.baseCoinType || !vault.quoteCoinType) continue;
